name: Von Gierke disease (glycogen storage disease type I)

reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / Scriver's Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease
clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive disorder of the terminal step of gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis; type Ia results from glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency (G6PC) and type Ib from a defect in the glucose-6-phosphate transporter (SLC37A4)
Presents in infancy with severe fasting hypoglycaemia, marked hepatomegaly, and a doll-like facies with truncal adiposity
The biochemical hallmark is fasting hypoglycaemia accompanied by lactic acidosis, hyperuricaemia, and hyperlipidaemia (raised triglycerides and cholesterol)
Type Ib additionally causes neutropenia and impaired neutrophil function, predisposing to recurrent infections and inflammatory bowel-like disease
Long-term complications include hepatic adenomas (with malignant potential), nephropathy with proteinuria, gout, growth retardation, and osteopenia
Cornerstone of management is maintaining euglycaemia with frequent feeds and uncooked cornstarch therapy while restricting galactose and fructose
Lactate can serve as an alternative cerebral fuel, which may partly protect the brain during hypoglycaemic episodes
reference.pathophysiology: Glycogen storage disease type I is caused by deficiency of the glucose-6-phosphatase system, which catalyses the final common step releasing free glucose from glucose-6-phosphate in both glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis. In type Ia the catalytic enzyme glucose-6-phosphatase is deficient, whereas in type Ib the microsomal transporter that moves glucose-6-phosphate into the endoplasmic reticulum is defective. As a result the liver, kidney, and intestine cannot release glucose during fasting, causing profound hypoglycaemia. Accumulating glucose-6-phosphate is diverted into glycolysis and the pentose phosphate and lipogenic pathways, generating excess lactate, uric acid, and triglycerides, while glycogen and fat accumulate in the liver and kidney. In type Ib, impaired glucose-6-phosphate transport also disturbs neutrophil function, producing neutropenia.
additionalDifferentials: Other hepatic glycogen storage diseases (types III, VI, IX)
Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase deficiency and other gluconeogenesis defects
Fatty acid oxidation disorders causing fasting hypoglycaemia
additionalInvestigations: Blood glucose, lactate, uric acid, and lipid profile during controlled fasting
Liver ultrasonography and surveillance imaging for hepatic adenomas
Renal function tests and urinalysis for proteinuria and microalbuminuria
Full blood count for neutropenia in suspected type Ib
Molecular genetic testing of G6PC and SLC37A4
Bone densitometry for osteopenia in longstanding disease
redFlags: Severe symptomatic hypoglycaemia with seizures or reduced consciousness
Severe lactic acidosis during metabolic decompensation
Rapidly enlarging or bleeding hepatic adenoma or features suggesting malignant transformation
Serious infection or gut inflammation in neutropenic type Ib patients
reference.prognosis: With meticulous dietary control to maintain euglycaemia, most patients survive into adulthood with good outcomes; long-term risks of hepatic adenoma with malignant potential, progressive nephropathy, and, in type Ib, infective complications remain the major determinants of prognosis.
pitfalls: Failing to prevent nocturnal hypoglycaemia by omitting overnight feeding or cornstarch
Overlooking neutropenia and its complications in type Ib
Missing surveillance for hepatic adenoma and renal disease during long-term follow-up
Giving galactose- or fructose-containing feeds that worsen the metabolic derangement
references: Scriver's The Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease
management: Maintain euglycaemia as the cornerstone: frequent daytime carbohydrate feeds with uncooked cornstarch, plus overnight continuous nasogastric or gastrostomy glucose feeds in infancy
Restrict galactose and fructose and provide a complex-carbohydrate-based diet to limit lactate and lipid generation, guided by a metabolic dietitian
Treat metabolic sequelae: allopurinol for hyperuricaemia and gout, lipid-lowering therapy with statins or fibrates for hyperlipidaemia, and citrate supplementation for nephrolithiasis
In type Ib, correct neutropenia and neutrophil dysfunction with granulocyte colony-stimulating factor and treat the inflammatory-bowel-like disease
Give prompt intravenous dextrose during intercurrent illness, vomiting or hypoglycaemia to avert acute metabolic decompensation and lactic acidosis
Structured surveillance with serial hepatic imaging for adenomas, renal function and urinary protein monitoring with an ACE inhibitor for proteinuric nephropathy, and bone densitometry for osteopenia
Refer for liver transplantation for hepatic adenoma with malignant transformation or intractable metabolic control, and offer renal transplantation for end-stage nephropathy
Provide genetic counselling for autosomal recessive inheritance with testing of at-risk relatives
